The House of Bourbon. When Henry IV ascended to the French throne in 1589, he brought internal peace to France after the Wars of Religion. His dynasty rose to become Europe's greatest of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.

Louis XIV, known as the Sun King, epitomized absolute monarchy. His famous motto was "I am the state," which defined centralized royal power for centuries. He built the Palace of Versailles, the grandest royal palace in Europe, and used it as both a seat of power and an instrument to control the nobility. He fought the War of Spanish Succession from 1701 to 1714, successfully establishing a Bourbon on the Spanish throne, though the effort weakened France's regional dominance.

The Bourbons ruled Spain from 1700 onwards as a cadet branch, and Spanish Bourbons remained on the throne into the modern era. But the dynasty's greatest tragedy came with Marie Antoinette and Louis XVI, the last Bourbon monarchs of France. They were executed during the French Revolution from 1789 to 1799. Their court culture of fashion, art, literature, and manners had become the model for European aristocracy, and the dynasty's fall marked the end of an age.
